subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Psychology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which of these is a directional (one-tailed) hypothesis?
options: Participants who revise will score higher than those who do not
There will be a relationship between the variables
Revision has no effect on scores
There will be a difference in test scores between the two groups
questions.explain: A directional hypothesis states the expected direction of the effect (e.g. 'higher than'), unlike a non-directional one.

questions.q: What does the null hypothesis predict?
options: That there is no difference or relationship, any result being due to chance
questions.explain: The null hypothesis predicts no difference or relationship; results are put down to chance.

questions.q: In an experiment, the variable the researcher manipulates is the:
questions.explain: The independent variable (IV) is manipulated by the researcher; the dependent variable (DV) is measured.

questions.q: A study tests whether caffeine affects reaction time. Reaction time is the:
questions.explain: Reaction time is measured as the outcome, so it is the dependent variable.

questions.q: Which sampling method gives every member of the target population an equal chance of selection?
questions.explain: In random sampling every member has an equal chance of being chosen, for example by drawing names.

questions.q: A researcher selects every 5th person from a list. This is:
questions.explain: Systematic sampling selects participants at fixed intervals (e.g. every nth person) from a list.

questions.q: A psychologist tests whoever happens to be in the canteen at lunchtime. This is:
questions.explain: Opportunity sampling uses people who are available and willing at the time; quick but often unrepresentative.

questions.q: Which experiment is conducted in a highly controlled, artificial setting?
questions.explain: A laboratory experiment is run in a controlled setting, giving high control but potentially low ecological validity.

questions.q: A researcher studies exam stress by comparing schools before and after a naturally occurring policy change they did not create. This is a:
questions.explain: In a natural experiment the IV varies naturally and is not manipulated by the researcher.

questions.q: In an independent groups design:
options: Different participants take part in each condition
Participants are matched on key variables
The same participants do every condition
questions.explain: Independent groups uses different participants in each condition, avoiding order effects but risking participant differences.

questions.q: A study uses the SAME people in both the 'quiet' and 'noisy' conditions. A key problem is:
options: Order effects such as practice or fatigue
questions.explain: Repeated measures (same participants) can create order effects like practice or fatigue, often reduced by counterbalancing.

questions.q: Which of the following is an ethical guideline set out for psychological research?
questions.explain: Informed consent is a core ethical requirement, alongside protection from harm, confidentiality and the right to withdraw.

questions.q: A participant becomes distressed but is told they may stop and leave at any time. This upholds their:
questions.explain: The right to withdraw lets participants leave the study at any point, protecting them from harm.

questions.q: Which is an example of quantitative data?
options: The number of words recalled in a test
questions.explain: Quantitative data is numerical (e.g. a score or count); qualitative data is descriptive, such as words or themes.

questions.q: A correlation coefficient of -0.85 shows:
questions.explain: A value near -1 shows a strong negative correlation: as one variable rises, the other falls.

questions.q: A study finds ice-cream sales and drownings both rise together. Why can we NOT say ice cream causes drownings?
options: Correlation does not prove cause and effect
questions.explain: Correlation shows a relationship, not causation; a third variable (hot weather) may explain both.

questions.q: The number 4500 written in standard form is:
questions.explain: Standard form is written as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten: 4500 = 4.5 x 10^3.

questions.q: The value 0.03682 rounded to 2 significant figures is:
questions.explain: The first two significant figures are 3 and 6; the next digit (8) rounds the 6 up to 7, giving 0.037.

questions.q: Which measure of central tendency is the most frequently occurring value?
questions.explain: The mode is the most common value; the median is the middle value and the mean is the arithmetic average.

questions.q: For the scores 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, what is the range?
questions.explain: The range is the highest value minus the lowest: 9 - 2 = 7.
